No.13

The Bodhisattva's View of Life and Death in "Futile Medical Treatment"

A faith-based reflection on the end of life and the pain of letting go, with a reading note on medical decisions.

Author's record · translated; the Chinese original is authoritative

Open in reading mode →

🔶Inquiry to Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva

I would like to ask the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas: in cases of futile medical treatment, should life support be withdrawn — for example, when the illness cannot be cured and the person would live on in a vegetative state? Or does the Bodhisattva consider this karmic obstruction, so that support should not be withdrawn and the retribution must be borne?

🔶The Bodhisattva's Teaching

What medicine cannot do
is not a sin;
what life cannot continue
is not a punishment.
If the form remains but awareness is gone,
if breath moves but the heart has departed,
to hold the body here by force
is not compassion,
nor is it filial piety.

Karma is not in the tube;
karma is in the heart.
If you keep them out of craving for life,
you add to suffering;
if you keep them because you cannot bear to part,
you bind everyone.
If, with a clear, compassionate heart that seeks nothing in exchange,
you let them go in peace,
this is not killing;
it is release.

But if the heart is confused, afraid, or seeking to escape blame,
then even if the tube is not withdrawn,
it still becomes heavy karma."

🔶Plain Rendering

When medicine has reached its limit and can do nothing more, this is no one's fault; when a life's span has ended and cannot go on, this is not a punishment sent from heaven. If a body is kept going only by machines, with no light of awareness left within; if breath still rises and falls by machine while the mind has long left this shell — then forcing this body to stay is neither compassion nor filial piety. The key to karma is not whether the life-support tube stays or goes, but the intention in the heart of the one who makes the decision.

If the family keeps the life going out of their own craving and unwillingness to part, it only adds needless suffering for the patient. If one hesitates only because "I cannot bear it", this attachment ties patient and family together in a prison of pain. If, with clear wisdom, pure compassion, and a heart that seeks nothing and trades nothing, you let the patient set out peacefully on the journey home — this is not killing, but "letting go, releasing your hold" — freeing them from the bonds of pain.

On the other hand, if the decision comes from panic, fear, or only wanting to avoid responsibility, then even if you choose not to remove the life support, that attachment forged from confusion and selfishness has itself already created heavy karma.
